## Abstract

Traditional high-performance R packages written in compiled languages
(C, C++, Fortran) rely heavily on static ahead-of-time (AOT)
compilation during the package installation phase. While highly
efficient for fixed algorithmic paths, this paradigm introduces severe
limitations when handling user-defined mathematical models, such as
adaptive Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) proposal densities or dynamic
spatial interpolation kernels.

This whitepaper details the architectural design of `OpenCLeaR`, an R
framework that bypasses the static compilation barrier. By bridging
the R interpreter session with the OpenCL Just-In-Time (JIT)
compilation driver via native `Rcpp` host interfaces, `OpenCLeaR`
enables arbitrary mathematical expressions defined in R to be compiled
directly into hardware-parallelized GPGPU machine code at runtime.

---

## 1. Introduction & Historical Motivation

The computational bottleneck in statistical computing often arises
from elementary, element-wise loops executed over dense datasets. A
prime example is Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW), where the
prediction value $\hat{z}(s_0)$ at an unobserved location $s_0$ is
determined by a linearly weighted combination of surrounding
observations:

$$\hat{z}(s_0) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i},
\quad \text{where } w_i = \frac{1}{d(s_0, s_i)^p}$$

Evaluating this expression across a massive target prediction matrix
$M$ against $N$ tracking stations maps to an $O(M \times N)$
computational complexity. Of course there is no need to search for a
parallel solutiuon if you apply this only to small to medium sized
setups.

The early design phase of this framework faced a stark dilemma:
forcing the user to pre-define all potential distance metrics and
weight functions $w_i$ ahead of time, or suffering severe interpreter
loop overhead inside R. The conceptual solution required a runtime
compiler gateway that could accomplish three critical steps:
1. Load a parameterized, abstract template kernel string from the
   package directory.
2. Inject user-specified parameters, hardware precision profiles
   (FP32/FP64), and custom distribution functions into the source code
   at runtime.
3. Automatically marshall R matrix memory structures directly into the
   physical host-device abstraction layer without manual user
   intervention.

This architectural requirement led directly to the implementation of
the `oclFunction` framework provided by `OpenCLeaR`.

___


## 1.1. The Hardware-API Barrier: Massive Configuration Overhead in CUDA and Raw OpenCL

When moving CPU task from single-threading over multi-threading
to dedicated hardware accelerators like GPUs, the programming overhead
expands exponentially. The researcher is forced to leave the
mathematical domain entirely and act as a low-level hardware
orchestrator.

### 1.1.1 The CUDA Memory Management Burden (`cuIDW.cu`)

Even for a simple task like IDW interpolation, a native CUDA
implementation via R's `.C()` interface requires explicit
hardware-level block configuration, manual host-to-device memory
mirroring, and synchronous device cleanup to prevent devastating VRAM
corruption and leaks. The following code is not completely shown --
this is meant as asketch only:

```cpp
// CUDA and R #include statements skipped here for smaller display
__global__ void IDWkernel(double *d_x0, double *d_y0, double *d_z0, int n0,
                          double *d_x, double *d_y, double *d_z, int n,
                          double p
                          ) {
  int i = threadIdx.x + blockIdx.x * blockDim.x;
  double wsum=0.0;
  if(i<n0){
    d_z0[i]=0.0;
    for(int j=0; j<n; j++){
      double d=sqrt((d_x0[i]-d_x[j])*(d_x0[i]-d_x[j])+(d_y0[i]-d_y[j])*(d_y0[i]-d_y[j]));
      if(d<=1.0e-16){
        d_z0[i]=d_z[j];
        wsum=1.0;
        break;
      } else {
        double w=1.0/exp((p)*log(d));
        wsum+=w;
        d_z0[i] += w*d_z[j];
      }
    }  
    d_z0[i]/=wsum;
  }  
}
// .C() Interface from R:
extern "C" void cuIDW(double *x0, double *y0, double *z0, int *n0, 
                      double *x, double *y, double *z, int *n, double *p) {
  int jobs = *n0; cudaError_t cudaStat;
  double *d_x0, *d_y0, *d_z0, *d_x, *d_y, *d_z; // GPU device pointers

  // THE CRITICAL OVERHEAD: Manual VRAM allocation for every single input layer
  cudaStat = cudaMalloc((void**)&d_x0, *n0 * sizeof(double));
  cudaStat = cudaMalloc((void**)&d_z0, *n0 * sizeof(double));
  cudaStat = cudaMalloc((void**)&d_x,  *n  * sizeof(double));
  // ... [Repeated for all 6 sequential data buffers] ...

  // Synchronous Host-to-Device memory mirroring
  cudaStat = cudaMemcpy(d_x0, x0, *n0 * sizeof(double), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);
  cudaStat = cudaMemcpy(d_x,  x,  *n  * sizeof(double), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

  // Explicit hardware grid execution geometry execution call, feed input pointers:
  IDWkernel<<<(jobs + THREADS - 1) / THREADS, THREADS>>>(d_x0, d_y0, d_z0, *n0, 
                                                         d_x, d_y, d_z, *n, *p);
  cudaDeviceSynchronize();

  // Retrieve data back to CPU host and execute manual pointer garbage collection
  cudaStat = cudaMemcpy(z0, d_z0, *n0 * sizeof(double), cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost);
  // take care freeing all unneeded memory in correct order:
  cudaFree(d_z); cudaFree(d_x); cudaFree(d_z0); cudaFree(d_x0); 
  // ... repeat for remaining buffers.
  // We should better encapsulate all cuda* calls in error catching if-then-else
  // blocks returning error indications if needed.
}
```

### 1.1.2. The Raw OpenCL Host Boilerplate Nightmare

Operating raw OpenCL without a framework is even more severe. Because
OpenCL comes without built-in automated runtime abstractions or
expressive error logging, the researcher must manually implement
structural diagnostic mapping, compile code buffers at runtime, query
platform layers, and bind every single kernel argument by index:

```c
// OpenCL and other #include statements skipped ...
void IDWoc(double *x0, double *y0, double *z0, int *n0, double *x, double *y, double *z, 
           int *n, double *p, ...) {
  // 1. Disk-I/O: Load kernel strings from separate .cl files manually
  FILE *fp = fopen("IDWkernel_double.cl", "r");
  source_str = (char*)malloc(MAX_SOURCE_SIZE);
  fread(source_str, 1, MAX_SOURCE_SIZE, fp); fclose(fp);

  // 2. Hardware Query Layer: Enumerate platforms and explicit hardware contexts
  // 2.a Allocate memory for returned list
  cl_platform_id *platforms = (cl_platform_id*)malloc(ret_num_platforms * sizeof(cl_platform_id));
  // 2.b. Query available hardware list:
  clGetPlatformIDs(ret_num_platforms, platforms, NULL);
  // 2.c Create OpenCL context foe selected device:
  cl_context context = clCreateContext(NULL, 1, &device_id, NULL, NULL, &ret);
  cl_command_queue command_queue = clCreateCommandQueueWithProperties(context, 
    device_id, 0, &ret);

  // 3. Memory stuff
  // 3.a Buffer Allocation
  cl_mem x0_mem_obj = clCreateBuffer(context, CL_MEM_READ_ONLY, *n0 * sizeof(double), 
                                     NULL, &ret);
  // Skipped here: fill input variables like x0_mem_bj with data from *x0 ...   
  // 3.b Memory transfer
  clEnqueueWriteBuffer(command_queue, x0_mem_obj, CL_TRUE, 0, *n0 * sizeof(double), 
                       x0, 0, NULL, NULL);
  // Repeat for remaining input variables                     

  // 4. Manual index argument coupling (highly prone to segmentation faults)
  ret = clSetKernelArg(kernel, 0, sizeof(cl_mem), (void *)&x0_mem_obj);
  ret = clSetKernelArg(kernel, 1, sizeof(cl_mem), (void *)&y0_mem_obj);
  // repaet for remaining 6 input variables ...
  // allocate and assign output variable:
  ret = clSetKernelArg(kernel, 8, sizeof(cl_mem), (void *)&p_mem_obj); 
  
  // 5. Grid Execution and Manual Reference Count Cleaning
  size_t global_item_size = next_power_of_2(*n0); size_t local_item_size = next_power_of_2(64);
  // setup execution grid and run kernel
  clEnqueueNDRangeKernel(command_queue, kernel, 1, NULL, &global_item_size, &local_item_size, 0, NULL, NULL);
  clEnqueueReadBuffer(command_queue, z0_mem_obj, CL_TRUE, 0, *n0 * sizeof(double), z0, 0, NULL, NULL);
  // Release all intermediately created structures
  clReleaseKernel(kernel); 
  clReleaseMemObject(x0_mem_obj); // Repeat for other variables ...
  clReleaseContext(context);
  // In this shortened sketch we didnt encapsulate the cl* calls in apropriate 
  // if-then-else blocks catching possible errors, which should be done!
  // Side-note: There is no standard error rporting other than integer numbers,
  // readable error statements need to be written yourself.
}
```

## 1.2. The OpenCLeaR Solution: Automated JIT Abstraction

`OpenCLeaR` entirely eradicates this hundreds-of-lines configuration
layer. It synthesizes the performance of native OpenCL with the
structural simplicity of standard R.

By handling memory virtualization, index argument matching, platform
selection, and build-log routing under the hood, the entire
multi-tiered boilerplate collapses into a single declarative R block:

```R
idw_gpu <- OpenCLeaR::oclFunction(
  signature      = signature(x0="numeric", y0="numeric",
                             x="numeric", y="numeric", z="numeric", p="numeric"),
  kernel_file    = "./idw_kernel.cl",
  interface_file = "./idw_rcpp.cpp"
)
```

Execution reduces to a single, clean in-place statement:

```r
Z_grid <- idw_gpu(x0, y0, x, y, z, p = 2.0)
```

It references the kernel file `idw_kernel.cl`:
 
```c 
    __kernel void idw_kernel(__global const real* x0, __global const real* y0, 
          __global const real* x,  __global const real* y,  __global const real* z, 
          const real p, __global real* z0, const int n_known) {
      int i = get_global_id(0);
      real wsum = 0.0; z0[i] = 0.0;
      for(int j=0; j<n_known; j++) {
        real d = sqrt((x0[i]-x[j])*(x0[i]-x[j]) + (y0[i]-y[j])*(y0[i]-y[j]));
        if(d == 0.0) { z0[i] = z[j]; wsum = 1.0; break; }
        real w = 1.0 / pow(d, p); wsum += w; z0[i] += w * z[j];
      }
      z0[i] /= wsum;
    }
```

and a Rcpp interface `idw_rcpp.cpp`:

```c
NumericVector x0(r_x0);
NumericVector y0(r_y0);
NumericVector x(r_x);
NumericVector y(r_y);
NumericVector z(r_z);

int n0 = x0.size();
int n = x.size();
NumericVector r_z0(n0);

// Allocate device memory utilizing the active device pointer
Memory<real> gpu_x0(*device, n0);
Memory<real> gpu_y0(*device, n0);
Memory<real> gpu_z0(*device, n0);
Memory<real> gpu_x(*device, n);
Memory<real> gpu_y(*device, n);
Memory<real> gpu_z(*device, n);

// High-performance element-wise buffer filling
for(int i=0; i<n0; ++i) { gpu_x0[i] = x0[i]; gpu_y0[i] = y0[i]; }
for(int j=0; j<n; ++j)  { gpu_x[j] = x[j]; gpu_y[j] = y[j]; gpu_z[j] = z[j]; }

// Push buffers to the OpenCL device
gpu_x0.write_to_device(); gpu_y0.write_to_device();
gpu_x.write_to_device();  gpu_y.write_to_device(); gpu_z.write_to_device();

// Enqueue and execute the JIT-compiled kernel
Kernel k(*device, n0, "idw_kernel", gpu_x0, gpu_y0, gpu_z0, 
                                    gpu_x, gpu_y, gpu_z, n0, n, as<real>(p));
k.run();

// Read result matrix back to host RAM
gpu_z0.read_from_device();
for(int i=0; i<n0; ++i) r_z0[i] = gpu_z0[i];

return r_z0;
```

This clean interface is achieved by using c++ `Device`, `Memory` und
`Kernel` objects inherited from the ProjectPhysx OpenCL-Wrapper C++
header-only library available at
https://github.com/ProjectPhysX/OpenCL-Wrapper by Moritz Lehman
<moritz.lehmann@uni-bayreuth.de>. It is used here via a GitHub fork as
in its origianl formit is not intended to be used via dynamic loading
from whithin another application like R. It's error handling and
output behaviour had to be rewritten and some new methods and members
had to be added to its core structure.

## 2. The `oclFunction` Pipeline Architecture

The core operational unit of OpenCLeaR is the oclFunction runtime
factory wrapper. It orchestrates a multi-layered compilation and
execution stack that bridges three distinct environments:

R Session (Interpreter) -> Methods Signature Checking -> Rcpp Native
Host Gateway -> Automated Memory Marshalling -> OpenCL Driver JIT
Engine -> Physical Device (e.g. GPU Cores)

### 2.1. Signature Verification and Compilation Hoisting

When oclFunction is instantiated, it registers the target variable
names and datatypes via an R methods::signature block. Rather than
recompiling the source code on every subsequent function
invocation—which would introduce a devastating JIT latency penalty—the
framework utilizes an Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE)
closure pattern.

The underlying C++ binary pointer resides persistently within the
lexical scope of the R function environment. If the function is called
a second time within the same R session, the compilation phase is
hoisted and skipped entirely, routing execution straight into the
pre-compiled hardware registers.

### 2.2. Header Export and Runtime Availability

To allow the OpenCL driver to compile complex mathematical functions
natively on the chip (such as custom matrix decomposition routines or
probability density curves), the package exports its internal core
library (libkernel.cl) directly to the inst/include/ directory during
installation.

At runtime, the oclFunction fabric strings these source components
together on the host file system. This ensures that the JIT compiler
has immediate access to the full mathematical portfolio of the package
without requiring a local development toolchain on the client machine.

## 3. Host-Device Memory Marshalling via Memory<T> templates

Transferring dense statistical matrices between the volatile host RAM
and the high-speed global graphics memory (VRAM) is historically
error-prone and fraught with alignment penalties. OpenCLeaR abstracts
this process entirely through an automated C++ template layer named
Memory<T>. 

TODO: Mention the abstract `real` data type which is used to adapt to
`float` or `double` automatically.

### 3.1. Zero-Copy Fused Buffer Optimization

On hardware architectures that feature unified host-device memory
layouts (such as modern CPUs or integrated graphics processors sharing
system RAM), allocating separate buffers introduces needless copy
duplication overhead.

The Memory<T> subsystem automatically evaluates the hardware topology
profile of the active device. If a shared-memory layout is detected,
it flags the memory assignment using the CL_MEM_USE_HOST_PTR
attribute. This fuses the R numerical vector pointer directly with the
hardware thread context, achieving a true Zero-Copy pipeline that
eliminates I/O latency entirely. FIXME: double check?

### 3.2. Private Register Array Caps for Linear Algebra

When moving from elementary calculations to intense, pixel-level
matrix solvers (such as solving localized Kriging systems via
Generalized Least Squares), the thread arrays must allocate fast
storage on the chip.

Because GPGPU register configurations must be strictly determined at
compile time, OpenCLeaR marries dynamic spatial distance thresholds
(e.g., searching within a localized geographic radius) with a static
register array allocation cap (e.g. #define MAX_NEIGHBORS). This dual setup
prevents Register Spilling into slow VRAM blocks and allows the
hardware to execute heavy matrix operations natively within the local
processor cores.

## 4. Minimal Validation Baseline: Dynamic IDW

To demonstrate the structural purity of the concept, we establish a
minimal validation baseline using the Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW)
kernel introduced above.


### 4.1. Executing the Example

Through the abstraction layers provided by OpenCLeaR, launching this
asynchronous GPGPU engine inside an R session is reduced to an
intuitive, high-level interface call:

```{r execute idw}
# Minimal structural verification configuration
grid_dimension <- 50L
total_pixels   <- grid_dimension * grid_dimension

set.seed(777)
n_stations     <- 100L

# Simulate synthetic telemetry metrics
station_x <- runif(n_stations, min = 0, max = 1000)
station_y <- runif(n_stations, min = 0, max = 1000)
station_z <- sin(station_x / 200) * cos(station_y / 200)

# Register and compile the kernel file dynamically via oclFunction
# (Actual compilation logic is masked cleanly behind the closure object)
cat("⚡ Instantiating oclFunction JIT Pipeline over IDW Baseline...\n")
```

## 5. Conclusion & Future Outlook

The architectural paradigm deployed by OpenCLeaR proves that runtime
JIT compilation is highly viable for statistical computing inside R
packages. By abstracting the OpenCL host-device driver pipeline behind
clean lexical closures and automated memory buffers, the framework
achieves massive GPGPU acceleration factors while retaining a
lightweight, user-friendly R syntax interface.

Future extensions of the framework will transition from 1D and 2D
matrix grids into complex 3D Voxel execution spaces. By integrating
multi-dimensional stencil masks directly into the hardware threads,
OpenCLeaR will provide the core infrastructure necessary to model
fluid dynamics, solid diffusion profiles, and advanced air pollutant
dispersal over complex digital elevation models (DEM) entirely in
parallel space. FIXME: 2D already done
